stops.name: Rome, Villa Savoia, the arrest
stops.campa: Summoned that afternoon to Villa Savoia expecting a routine audience, Mussolini is told by Victor Emmanuel III that the war is lost, that Marshal Badoglio will form the next government, and that he is, in the king's own words, the most hated man in Italy. Stepping outside in a daze after twenty minutes he is stopped by carabinieri, bundled into a Red Cross ambulance under armed guard, and driven away into a captivity that will move him from barracks to island to mountain over the following seven weeks.

stops.name: Campo Imperatore, the Gran Sasso rescue
stops.campa: Held now at the Hotel Campo Imperatore high on the Gran Sasso, reachable only by cable car, Mussolini watches German gliders crash-land on the mountain plateau below the hotel windows. A hundred SS troopers and paratroopers under Otto Skorzeny overwhelm the guard without a shot fired, and Mussolini is flown out in a tiny Storch aircraft that barely clears the cliff edge on takeoff. He is not a free man returning to power but a rescued prisoner, and both he and Hitler already know which of the two states now truly owns the other.
stops.quote: I knew that my friend Adolf Hitler would not abandon me.
stops.quote_source: Attributed by Otto Skorzeny, Skorzeny's Special Missions (1950)

stops.name: Rastenburg, East Prussia, meeting Hitler at the Wolfsschanze
stops.campa: Flown by way of Vienna and Munich to Hitler's forest headquarters in East Prussia, Mussolini meets the ally who ordered his rescue and now dictates his future. Hitler wants a Fascist government restored in the German-occupied north to hold Italy in the war and shield the Reich's exposed southern flank. Mussolini, sick, visibly aged, and without an army, an illusion, or any real choice left him, agrees to head the state Hitler names for him, no longer a sovereign ally but an instrument of the occupying power.

stops.name: Gargnano, Palazzo Feltrinelli, the Republic proclaimed
stops.campa: The Italian Social Republic is proclaimed, its ministries scattered in towns around Lake Garda, its nominal capital the small lakeside town of Salò, though Mussolini himself lodges and works under permanent SS guard at the requisitioned Villa Feltrinelli in Gargnano. He revives on paper the old syndicalist program of 1919, land and factories promised to the workers in a socialization decree meant to prove fascism was never merely capital's servant, even as German officers and Italian partisans in the surrounding mountains decide the republic's real business without consulting him.

stops.name: Verona, Castelvecchio, the trial and Ciano's execution
stops.campa: At Castelvecchio a special tribunal tries the Grand Council members who voted against him the previous July, among them his own son-in-law Galeazzo Ciano, husband of his daughter Edda. Found guilty of treason in a proceeding whose verdict is fixed before it opens, Ciano and four others are shot in the fortress ditch on the eleventh of January, tied to chairs and shot in the back by the executioners' own choice of humiliation. Edda's plea for clemency, smuggled out with Ciano's diaries as her price, reaches Mussolini's desk one day too late, by design; he lets the sentence stand.

stops.name: Dongo, the capture
stops.campa: As the Republic collapses and Milan's partisans rise, Mussolini flees north toward Switzerland or the Alps within a retreating German convoy, Claretta Petacci following in a car of her own. At Musso a roadblock of the 52nd Garibaldi Brigade stops the column; the next morning at Dongo a searching partisan recognizes the unmistakable jutting chin of a soldier slumped in a greatcoat among the German trucks. We have got Mussolini, the cry goes up along the lakeshore; twenty-one years of dictatorship end at a fuel-truck checkpoint on the road to Como.

stops.name: Giulino di Mezzegra, Villa Belmonte, the execution
stops.campa: Held overnight with Petacci at a farmhouse above Bonzanigo, Mussolini is brought down the following afternoon before the gate of Villa Belmonte by partisans acting, they say, on the National Liberation Committee's order. He and Petacci are shot against the villa's low stone wall; accounts of his final seconds disagree, some claiming he bared his chest and asked to be struck there, others that no words passed between the condemned and their executioners at all. The bodies are loaded that night, with others shot the same day, onto a truck bound for Milan.

stops.name: Milan, Piazzale Loreto, the bodies displayed
stops.campa: Before dawn the bodies of Mussolini, Petacci and fifteen other executed fascists are dumped in the Piazzale Loreto, the same square where fascist militia had left the bodies of fifteen executed partisans on public view the previous August. The crowd that gathers through the morning kicks, spits on and mutilates the dead Duce; by afternoon he and Petacci are strung up by the feet from the girders of a bombed Esso filling station, an image that closes, for the world's cameras, twenty-three years of Fascist Italy.
